newsitem.title: USA: About 90 species of U.S. birds in decline.
newsitem.headline: About 90 species of U.S. birds in decline.

text.p: More and more U.S. birds, from tiny hummingbirds to long-legged American bittern, are at risk, according to a study released on Monday.
About 90 bird species -- 14 percent of all U.S. breeding species -- are in decline or danger, the National Audubon Society said in its "Watch List" count.

"With 90 species listed, including many birds familiar to most Americans, the Watch List is nothing less than a warning cry," said John Flicker, president of the environmental group named after famed ornithologist Jean Jacques Audubon.
The birds the group listed are not yet on the Endangered Species List and Audubon wants to make sure they never are.

"Birds are an indicator group and many on the Watch List show abnormal declines. We hope this accounting serves as a wake-up call to all people who are concerned about the health of the environment, not only for birds, but for themselves and their children," Flicker said.
The list was compiled by scientists and volunteers. Many of the species are facing loss of habitat, probably the single greatest danger to wildlife.

From the U.S. Northeast, birds in trouble include the bright yellow golden-winged warbler. The number of curved bill thrashers, which nest in cactus plants and desert shrubs, has dropped by four percent in the Southwest since the mid-1960s, while in the Northwest the yellow-headed blackbird population has declined 33 percent since the early 1980s, largely as a result of draining wetlands.
